findings.source_passage: where infantileness of ease undulates through a Titanism of power. On the contrary, those motions derive their most appalling beauty from it.
findings.source_locator: paragraph on strength and grace, after 'does not tend to cripple'
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'infantileness of ease undulates through a Titanism of power' is one of the most rhetorically distinctive and critically cited sentences in the chapter; its oxymoronic structure and coined Latinism are signature Melville and are entirely lost in the draft's flat paraphrase 'nor does strength cripple grace; rather it bestows it.'
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the verbatim phrase 'infantileness of ease undulates through a Titanism of power' and the following sentence about 'most appalling beauty'; they are too distinctive to paraphrase away.

findings.source_passage: As devout Eckerman lifted the linen sheet from the naked corpse of Goethe, he was overwhelmed with the massive chest of the man, that seemed as a Roman triumphal arch.
findings.source_locator: paragraph on strength and beauty, between Hercules and Angelo
findings.why_it_matters: The Eckermann/Goethe anecdote is a critically noted biographical-aesthetic set-piece used to anchor Melville's argument about strength and beauty; its complete absence removes an important interpretive keystone and a memorable, highly distinctive passage.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Eckermann/Goethe sentence; even a compressed version must name Eckermann lifting the sheet from Goethe's corpse and the image of the massive chest as a Roman triumphal arch.

findings.source_passage: the soft, curled, hermaphroditical Italian pictures, in which his idea has been most successfully embodied; these pictures, so destitute as they are of all brawniness
findings.source_locator: paragraph on strength and beauty, near end, the critique of Italian religious painting
findings.why_it_matters: 'Hermaphroditical' is a critically loaded and period-distinctive term Melville uses deliberately; the draft reduces this to 'soft Italian Sons,' losing the rhetorical charge and the specific interpretive content about gender and artistic representation.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'hermaphroditical Italian pictures' and the phrase 'destitute of all brawniness' to preserve the voice and the interpretive force of the passage.

findings.source_passage: if you noticed the light wreath of vapor from the spiracle at his other extremity, you would think that that was the smoke from the touch-hole.
findings.why_it_matters: The spiracle/touch-hole simile is a characteristically whimsical and vivid Melvillean image completing the lobtailing description; the draft cuts it entirely, reducing the fourth motion to mere statement of concussion.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the touch-hole/spiracle image to complete the lobtailing passage as Melville wrote it.

findings.source_passage: if in the Dantean, the devils will occur to you; if in that of Isaiah, the archangels.
findings.source_locator: Fifth motion (peaking flukes) paragraph, after the Satan/Baltic image
findings.why_it_matters: The Dante/Isaiah interpretive frame — that what one sees in the flukes depends on one's spiritual mood — is a key interpretive statement about the whole book's hermeneutic; its absence removes philosophically significant content.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Dantean/Isaiah sentence; it is short and carries heavy interpretive weight about the relativity of symbolic perception.

findings.source_passage: So in dreams, have I seen majestic Satan thrusting forth his tormented colossal claw from the flame Baltic of Hell.
findings.source_locator: Fifth motion (peaking flukes) paragraph, after 'shoot out of view'
findings.why_it_matters: This Satan/Baltic of Hell simile is one of the most vivid and tonally distinctive lines in the chapter, establishing the sublime/infernal register that then contrasts with the archangels/Isaiah alternative; its omission flattens a crucial rhetorical and imaginative peak.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Satan sentence verbatim; it is indispensable to the movement from infernal to divine in the peaking flukes passage.

summary: The draft commits one certain high-severity loss (the 'infantileness of ease undulates through a Titanism of power' sentence and the Eckermann/Goethe anecdote) and four medium-severity losses including the Satan/Baltic image, the Dantean/Isaiah frame, the hermaphroditical Italian pictures phrasing, and the spiracle/touch-hole simile, collectively gutting the chapter's most distinctive rhetorical and interpretive passages.
